title: Resource Requests & Limits 📏
description: Learn how to declare resource needs and constraints for your containers.

slides.title: Why Resources Matter 🧐
slides.content:
# Keep the cluster balanced

Every container consumes CPU and memory. Without telling Kubernetes how much it needs, the scheduler can’t place Pods effectively, and one Pod could starve others.

**Requests** – the minimum guaranteed resources for a container. The scheduler uses this to find a suitable node.
**Limits** – the maximum resources a container can use. Exceeding the memory limit results in OOMKill; exceeding the CPU limit causes throttling.

quizData.question: What does a CPU request guarantee?

options.text: The container will get exactly that much CPU
The container is scheduled onto a node with at least that much CPU available
The container can never use more than that
The node’s CPU is reserved exclusively for this container

quizData.explanation: Requests are used for scheduling. The container may burst above request if resources are available.

slides.title: CPU and Memory Units 📐
slides.content:
## How to specify them

- **CPU**: measured in **millicores** (m). `100m` = 0.1 CPU core. `1` = 1 whole core.
- **Memory**: bytes. `Mi` (mebibytes), `Gi` (gibibytes). `512Mi` ≈ 512 megabytes.

Example:
```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "250m"
    memory: "64Mi"
  limits:
    cpu: "500m"
    memory: "128Mi"
```

slides.title: Full Container Spec with Resources
slides.codeSnippet:
containers:
- name: app
  image: myapp:1.0
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: "100m"
      memory: "128Mi"
    limits:
      cpu: "500m"
      memory: "256Mi"

slides.title: What Happens Without Requests/Limits? 🤷
slides.content:
## The wild west

- Without **requests**, the scheduler may place too many Pods on a node, causing resource starvation.
- Without **limits**, a memory leak can consume all node memory, and the kubelet will OOMKill the container (or another container).
- **Best practice**: always set both for production workloads.

quizData.question: If a container exceeds its memory limit, what does Kubernetes do?

options.text: Evict the Pod to another node
Allow it but log a warning

quizData.explanation: Memory is an incompressible resource; exceeding the limit leads to an OOM kill.

slides.title: Quality of Service (QoS) Classes 🏅
slides.content:
## Kubernetes prioritises Pods

Based on requests and limits, Pods get a QoS class:
- **Guaranteed** – every container has equal requests and limits (cpu+memory). Highest priority.
- **Burstable** – at least one container has a request or limit but not all are equal.
- **BestEffort** – no requests or limits. First to be evicted under memory pressure.

Use `kubectl describe pod` to see the QoS class.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges

Namespaces can enforce resource policies with ResourceQuotas (limits total resources) and LimitRanges (default requests/limits for containers that don't specify them).

quizData.question: Which QoS class gives the strongest guarantee against eviction?
quizData.explanation: Guaranteed Pods have the highest priority and are evicted only when absolutely necessary.
